hints: Remember that the power each concentration is raised to in the rate equation is its order, not its stoichiometric coefficient.
walkthrough:
Translate order into powers**
Think of order as the instruction for the rate equation. First order in $\text{NO}$ means you write $[\text{NO}]^1$, and first order in $\text{O}_3$ means you write $[\text{O}_3]^1$. Put them together with $k$ in front to get rate $= k[\text{NO}][\text{O}_3]$.

hints: Start by writing the rate expression from (a)(i) and substitute $k = 11500$ and both concentrations $= 1.20 \times 10^{-6} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.
Check how the units of $k$ combine with $\text{mol}^2 \text{ dm}^{-6}$ to leave the correct units for rate.
walkthrough:
Substitute into the rate equation**
You have rate $= k[\text{NO}][\text{O}_3]$. Both concentrations are the same, so this is really useful to see clearly:
$$\text{rate} = 11500 \times (1.20 \times 10^{-6}) \times (1.20 \times 10^{-6})$$
$$\text{rate} = 11500 \times 1.44 \times 10^{-12} = 1.656 \times 10^{-8}$$
Round to three significant figures to match the data to give $1.66 \times 10^{-8}$.

Sort out the units**
Concentration times concentration gives $\text{mol}^2 \text{ dm}^{-6}$. Multiply by $k$ in $\text{mol}^{-1} \text{dm}^3 \text{s}^{-1}$ and the $\text{mol}^{-1}$ cancels one $\text{mol}$, the $\text{dm}^3$ cancels part of $\text{dm}^{-6}$. You are left with $\text{mol dm}^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$, which is exactly what you expect for rate.

Final answer: rate $= 11500 \times (1.20 \times 10^{-6})^2 = 1.66 \times 10^{-8}$
units $= \text{mol dm}^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$

hints: Recall which overall order gives a constant half-life, and work out the overall order here from $1 + 1$.
walkthrough:
Link half-life to overall order**
Picture what constant half-life really means. It is a special fingerprint of first order reactions only. Here order in $\text{NO}$ is $1$ and order in $\text{O}_3$ is $1$, so overall order $= 1 + 1 = 2$. A second order reaction has a half-life that increases as concentration falls, so the graph of $[\text{NO}]$ against time will not show a constant half-life.

Final answer: prediction: does not show constant half-life
explanation: overall order is second order, not first order, constant half-life is only shown by first order reactions

hints: Think about what zero order means for the effect of concentration on rate as $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ is used up over time.
walkthrough:
See why rate stays flat**
Zero order means rate does not depend on $[\text{N}_2\text{O}]$ at all. Even though $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ is being used up, the rate stays exactly the same. On a rate against time plot that looks like a horizontal straight line, parallel to the time axis, starting above the origin.
Final answer: Horizontal straight line parallel to time axis, at positive rate, showing rate is constant and independent of concentration.

hints: If the same amount reacts per unit time because rate is constant, think about what shape that gives for concentration falling with time.
walkthrough:
Connect constant rate to concentration fall**
If rate is constant, $[\text{N}_2\text{O}]$ falls by the same amount every second. That steady drop gives a straight line sloping down. So draw a straight line with a negative gradient from the initial concentration on the y-axis towards the time axis.
Final answer: Straight line with negative constant gradient, starting at initial $[\text{N}_2\text{O}]$ on y-axis.

hints: Start by picturing gaseous $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ molecules arriving at the solid platinum surface, what is the name for binding to active sites?
Think about what happens to the strength of the $\text{N-N}$ and $\text{N-O}$ bonds once the molecule is held on the surface.
Finish by considering how $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ leave the surface so the site can be reused.
walkthrough:
Adsorption onto active sites**
Imagine $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ gas molecules hitting the platinum wire. Because this is heterogeneous, catalyst and reactants are in different phases. The $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ molecules bind to active sites on the Pt surface. This is adsorption, forming weak surface bonds.

Weakening of bonds**
Once held on the surface, electron density shifts between Pt and the adsorbed molecule. This weakens the bonds inside $\text{N}_2\text{O}$, so less energy is needed to break them. In other words, the reaction now follows a new route of lower activation energy. Reactants are also held close together in the correct orientation.

Reaction then desorption**
Decomposition to $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ happens on the surface, then the products desorb, meaning they detach and diffuse away. That leaves the active site clean and free for another $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ molecule, so the platinum is unchanged at the end.

Final answer: Reactants are adsorbed onto active sites on platinum surface.
Adsorption weakens bonds in $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ and lowers activation energy.
Reaction occurs on surface followed by desorption of $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ products, freeing active sites.

hints: Compare the large number of $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ molecules with the very small platinum surface, what must be true about the active sites?
walkthrough:
Spot surface saturation**
Think of the platinum wire as having only a tiny number of parking spaces, while there is a huge crowd of $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ molecules waiting. Every active site is full at all times. Adding more $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ cannot increase the rate because there is nowhere extra for it to adsorb, so concentration has no effect and the kinetics are zero order.
Final answer: All active sites on the platinum surface are occupied / surface is saturated, so rate depends only on surface area, not on $[\text{N}_2\text{O}]$.
